4.text: The Chukchee shamans do not practise the ventriloquistic art in the

5.text: outer tent in daylight. I did indeed hear one or two shamans boast of their

6.text: ability to call “separate voices” in the outer tent, and that some of these

7.text: voices talked to them out of the fire of the hearth; but they were never able

8.text: to make good these pretensions. One shaman, since dead, was said to have

9.text: performed such a feat; but the “separate voices” of his calling were heard

10.text: all the time very near to his knees, and he had even to stoop down to talk

11.text: with them. The hearth, however, is considered to be a fit entrance for keˊlet.

12.text: In Koryak tales the kaˊmak (evil spirit) comes into the house out of the fire

13.text: of the hearth:¹ therefore the hearth is surrounded with a circle of stones,

14.text: which are supposed also by the Chukchee to keep off the keˊlet. When a

15.text: keˊlᴇ wants to enter, the stones turn into inaccessible mountains, and enclose

16.text: the fire as a small world apart.

17.text: The “spirits” called by the shamans during the ceremonials in the outer

18.text: tent can manifest themselves only through the body of the shaman, who in

19.text: due time begins to utter the same gibbering noises and hysterical cries that

20.text: have already been described. The shamans also imitate the voices of animals

21.text: and birds, stamp the ground with their feet, and jump about violently, foaming

22.text: at the mouth, and even breaking such things as may come within reach of

23.text: their hands. A shaman whose body is entered by a keˊlᴇ loses the faculty

24.text: of human speech, and may express his wishes either by gestures or by

25.text: gibbering unintelligible noises. When the keˊlᴇ is an animal, the shaman

26.text: tries to act accordingly. He crawls on all-fours, grunting, and gnashing his

27.text: teeth. I was told several times that some of the shamans even put on a

28.text: bear or a wolf skin, taken off with the claws and the skull.²

29.text: Sometimes a keˊlᴇ who entered the body of a shaman on the day of the

30.text: ceremonial is bent on mischief, and, among other things, seeks to destroy the

31.text: life which is under his temporary power.

32.text: Among the Reindeer Chukchee on the Wolverene River I knew a man

33.text: by the name of Akɪˊmlᴀkê (“Marrowless”), who gave himself out as a shaman,

34.text: though the people usually did not pay much attention to his claim. At the

35.text: times of ceremonials, Akɪˊmlᴀkê would pretend that a keˊlᴇ had entered his

36.text: body and was bent on destroying his life. He would usually spend a part

37.text: of his time crawling about in search of a knife. The women of his house,

38.text: however, well aware of this holy-day custom of his, usually took care to

39.text: conceal all knives and other sharp weapons. Once, at a thanksgiving cere-

40.text: monial at which I was present, he began his usual search, and came to me,
